screens.title: Scaling the Services
screens.narratorSegment: As usage grows, a single server cannot reliably handle millions of redirects or large paste uploads. In this lesson we focus on two complementary strategies for horizontal scaling: load balancing, which spreads incoming requests across many app servers to improve performance and availability, and sharding, which splits database data across multiple servers so storage and query work scales. You will learn when to use different load balancing algorithms such as round robin or least connection, and why the redirect service often needs a different approach than your A P I endpoints. For storage, we explain hash-based, range-based, and directory-based sharding and trade-offs for short codes, paste IDs, and user-owned data. Each topic includes concrete configuration and code examples that map directly to URL Shortener and Pastebin patterns. By the end, you should be able to choose a load balancing algorithm for a specific bottleneck, design a sharding key for efficient lookups, and anticipate challenges like hot spots or re-sharding costs. Think about which part of your service is most read-heavy and which part grows in storage — that distinction guides both load balancing and sharding choices.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Scaling the Services

Scaling the Services

Focus: practical patterns for distributing requests and distributing data so URL Shortener and Pastebin scale with traffic and storage.

In this lesson
When and how to use load balancers to spread requests and improve availability.
Data strategy
Sharding patterns for storing short codes and paste content across multiple database nodes.
Challenges
Hot spots, cross-shard queries, and re-sharding trade-offs you must anticipate.
Topic — Load Balancer

A single point that routes incoming requests to multiple app servers to balance load and detect failures.

Topic — Sharding

Splitting a logical database across multiple physical servers to scale storage and queries horizontally.

Topic — Trade-offs

Design choices affect complexity like cross-shard queries, re-sharding cost, and hotspot risk.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Concept map — how requests and data split
Load Balancer
Distributes requests for both API and redirect services, detects unhealthy servers, and reduces latency.
Redirect Service
High-volume, read-heavy path for GET short codes; often served by identical stateless servers behind a fast balancer.
Shards
Multiple database instances, each holding a subset of records based on a shard key like short_code or paste_id.
Hot Spots
Uneven distribution from a poor shard key or popular user can overload a shard; plan mitigation strategies.
Key Takeaway

Combine appropriate load balancing for requests with an intentional sharding strategy for storage to achieve reliable horizontal scale.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on skills you can apply when scaling a web service. First, you will understand the operational role of load balancers: how they distribute traffic, detect failures, and improve availability for A P I and redirect paths. For example, you will see how a redirect service that receives millions of GET requests benefits from a simple round-robin distribution across identical servers. Second, you will evaluate load balancing algorithms and match them to workload characteristics, such as preferring least-connection for long-lived connections. Third, you will explain database sharding — why it’s necessary to partition a large dataset across multiple servers and how that affects query patterns and availability. Finally, you will design a sharding strategy tailored to URL Shortener and Pastebin data, weighing shard-key choices like short_code versus user_id and considering trade-offs around hot spots and re-sharding. Each objective maps to a competency milestone so you can check that you can choose an algorithm, justify a shard key, and plan mitigation for common sharding challenges.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide frames each learning goal as a practical skill you can apply immediately. You should be able to evaluate logs and metrics to decide whether a balancer should use least-connection or round-robin, and to explain why IP-hash creates client stickiness but does not balance load by itself. You will also be able to draft a sharding plan: choose a shard key, describe how records map to shards, and outline a path for re-sharding. Practical mastery means not just naming techniques, but producing a short plan and explaining trade-offs to an engineer or manager.

screens.title: Horizontal Scaling: Load Balancing vs Sharding
screens.narratorSegment: Horizontal scaling is the practice of adding more machines to handle increasing traffic and data. There are two distinct but complementary techniques: load balancing and sharding. Load balancing distributes incoming requests across multiple application servers so no single server becomes a bottleneck; it addresses requests per second and availability. Sharding splits the database horizontally so each database instance stores only a subset of rows; it addresses storage, input and output, and per-query work. For an URL Shortener, think of load balancers keeping redirect servers evenly busy while sharding keeps short-code records distributed across multiple database nodes. A common misconception is to treat them as interchangeable; they solve different problems. If your app servers are saturated but the database is fine, tune the balancer or add app instances. If your DB disk, input and output, or query latency is the limit, sharding is needed. A concrete example: redirect traffic is extremely read-heavy and benefits from many identical stateless servers behind a balancer, while paste content with large blobs may require shards to distribute storage across machines. Key takeaway: use load balancing for request-level scaling, and sharding for data-level scaling — both together let the system grow without a single point becoming a hard limit.

keyIdea.title: Two levels of scale
keyIdea.text: Load balancers scale request throughput; sharding scales storage and query capacity. Use both when traffic and data grow together.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Horizontal Scaling
Definition

Load Balancing and Sharding

Load balancing spreads incoming requests across many app servers. Sharding partitions database rows across multiple database servers. Together they remove single-node limits.

Concrete example
Millions of short-code redirects served by identical stateless servers behind a balancer; paste blobs stored across multiple DB shards to keep per-shard storage bounded.
Common misconception
Adding more app servers always solves latency. Not if the database is the bottleneck — you may need sharding instead.
Key Takeaway

Match the scaling technique to the constrained resource: CPU/connections -> balancer/app instances; storage/I/O -> sharding.

Comparison
Load Balancer
Targets request distribution, failover, and per-request latency reduction.
Sharding
Targets data distribution, storage limits, and per-query performance on smaller datasets.
Analogy
Load balancer: traffic director at an intersection. Shard: divide a library into smaller rooms so books fit and are found quickly.
Check your understanding
  • If app servers show high CPU but DB latency is low, which scaling technique do you pick?
  • When many users request the same short code repeatedly, what problem might arise in sharding?
  • How do session persistence requirements influence balancer algorithm choice?

screens.title: What a Load Balancer Does
screens.narratorSegment: A load balancer's job is simple to state but critical to implement correctly. Its primary goals are threefold: distribute incoming work so no server is overwhelmed, detect unhealthy servers and route traffic to healthy instances, and reduce end-to-end response times by spreading requests. For URL Shortener and Pastebin, different endpoints have different characteristics: POST endpoints are write-heavy and less frequent, whereas GET redirect requests are extremely frequent and latency-sensitive. A typical process is: accept client connection, consult routing rules or algorithm, forward the request to a chosen backend, and monitor backend health to remove failing servers from rotation. A common operational pitfall is paying too much attention to a simple round-robin policy when backends have different capacities or when connection durations vary. For long-lived or uneven workloads, prefer least-connection or least-response-time. Another misconception is that stickiness is always needed; for stateless redirect servers, stickiness adds overhead without benefit. Practically, monitoring metrics like active connections, response time percentiles, and error rates helps you pick and tune the balancer behavior. Ask yourself: what metric best indicates an overloaded backend for this endpoint?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Load Balancer Responsibilities
Process Flow
1. Accept client request
Connection arrives at the balancer for an API or redirect path.
2. Choose backend
Use an algorithm and health info to select a server.
3. Forward and monitor
Proxy request and watch response times and failures to update health state.
Example metric checks
  • Active connections per server
  • 95th percentile response time
  • Error rate and TCP connection failures
Concrete scenario
The redirect service receives bursty traffic. If some servers have more long-lived connections, Round Robin will overload them. Switching to least-connection routes new requests to underutilized machines and evens out load.
Common mistake
Assuming every endpoint should use the same algorithm. Use least-connection for uneven or long-lived connections; round robin is fine for identical, short-lived stateless requests.

screens.title: Load Balancing Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right load balancing algorithm depends on the workload and backend heterogeneity. Round Robin cycles sequentially and is simple and fair when servers are identical and connection durations are short. Weighted Round Robin improves on that by assigning higher weights to more powerful servers, useful when you have mixed instance sizes. Least Connection routes to the server with the fewest active connections and is strong for long-lived sessions or when backend processing times vary. Least Response Time chooses the backend with the fastest recent responses and is effective when you want to minimize latency at the cost of more measurement. IP Hash maps a client’s IP to a server to provide stickiness; it ensures the same client frequently hits the same backend, but it does not balance capacity across clients. For our services: prefer least-connection or least-response-time for application servers because they react to real load. For redirect service, if servers are identical, round robin or weighted round robin works well because the path is stateless and extremely high-volume. A typical misconception is thinking IP Hash solves load imbalances — it often creates uneven distribution if client IPs are not uniformly distributed. Always validate algorithm choice with connection and latency metrics before committing.

keyIdea.text: Match algorithm to connection patterns and heterogeneity: least-connection for variable durations, round robin for identical stateless servers, IP hash for stickiness only.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Load Balancing Algorithms
Algorithms at a glance
Round Robin
Simple sequential distribution. Great for identical, short-lived requests.
Weighted Round Robin
Assign more traffic to stronger servers by weight.
Least Connection
Send requests to server with fewest active connections; useful for long-lived or uneven workloads.
Least Response Time
Choose backend with the fastest observed responses to minimize latency.
IP Hash
Maps client IP to a server for stickiness; does not guarantee even capacity distribution.
Suitability matrix
Redirect Service
High-volume, stateless. Use Round Robin for identical servers; Weighted Round Robin if capacity differs.
API Service (POST)
Write-heavy endpoints with variable load. Least Connection or Least Response Time better reflect real capacity.
Misconception
IP Hash will balance traffic — not true unless client IPs are evenly distributed; it mainly provides stickiness.
Pro tip
Start with a simple algorithm in production but collect connection and latency metrics so you can switch to a more adaptive algorithm when needed.

screens.title: Example: Conceptual Nginx Load Balancer Config
screens.narratorSegment: A conceptual Nginx configuration helps translate algorithm choices into routing rules. The upstream block defines backend pools; you can list servers and choose a balancing mode such as least_conn or leave it as default round robin. In practice, you would create separate upstream pools for A P I endpoints and redirect endpoints because their load characteristics differ. The config shown in the lesson is conceptual: it demonstrates grouping A P I servers under one upstream and redirect servers under another, optionally enabling least_conn for the redirect pool if long-lived connections are expected. Real configurations include health checks and timeouts to withdraw unhealthy hosts. A common misconception is to copy-paste a simple upstream without health checks — this can route traffic to a failed host and increase client errors. Use active or passive health checks and metrics export from the balancer to your monitoring system. This example is not production-ready but illustrates how to map services to pools and algorithms so your architecture documentation directly informs your load balancer rules. Example: Conceptual Nginx Load Balancer Config means separate upstream pools per service and choose a mode per pool; ensure health checks are configured to avoid routing to failed servers.. In practical terms, how upstream blocks map endpoints to backend pools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Nginx Config Example
Conceptual configuration
http {
    upstream backend_api {
        server api_server_1.example.com;
        server api_server_2.example.com;
    }

    upstream backend_redirect {
        least_conn; # Use least connection for redirect service
        server redirect_server_1.example.com;
        server redirect_server_2.example.com;
    }

    server {
        listen 80;
        location /api/v1/shorten {
            proxy_pass http://backend_api;
        }
        location /api/v1/pastes {
            proxy_pass http://backend_api;
        }
        location ~ ^/[a-zA-Z0-9]{7}$ {
            proxy_pass http://backend_redirect;
        }
    }
}
Explanation
  • Separate upstreams let you tune algorithms per service and scale pools independently.
  • Using least_conn in backend_redirect helps when connection durations vary; if servers are identical, round robin is acceptable.
  • Always add health checks and timeouts in production to avoid routing to unhealthy backends.
Common mistake
Not tuning upstream settings per service. One-size-fits-all leads to underutilized or overloaded pools.

screens.title: Database Sharding: What and Why
screens.narratorSegment: Sharding, or horizontal partitioning, splits a logical database so each shard stores a subset of rows. This lowers per-shard storage and input and output, allows more R A M use per working set, and spreads query work across machines. Key reasons to shard include overcoming single-server limits on C P U, memory, input and output, and disk. For Pastebin, content size variability and storage growth make sharding essential once a single instance approaches capacity. For URL Shortener, lookups by short_code are the most frequent operation; sharding lets you keep each lookup fast by searching a smaller dataset on a shard. A typical misconception is that sharding automatically simplifies queries; it often complicates them because cross-shard queries require coordination or aggregation. Another operational cost is re-sharding: moving data when you add or remove shards. Plan for that complexity early by choosing a sharding scheme that balances even distribution with operational manageability. The practical approach is to pick a key like short_code or paste_id and implement a deterministic mapping to a shard so lookups are efficient. Think about how you will handle queries that must gather data from many shards — that design decision impacts read paths, indexes, and denormalized secondary stores.

keyIdea.text: Sharding trades increased operational complexity for the ability to scale storage and query capacity beyond a single machine.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Database Sharding
Core definition

What is sharding?

Horizontal partitioning of data across multiple database servers where each shard holds a subset of the total dataset determined by a shard key.

Why shard?
  • Overcome single-server CPU, memory and storage limits.
  • Improve query performance by reducing per-shard dataset size.
  • Increase availability because a single shard failure does not lose all data.
Operational notes
Sharding reduces per-node resource pressure but introduces cross-shard query complexity and re-sharding costs. Plan for schema designs that avoid frequent cross-shard transactions.
Misconception
Sharding fixes all performance issues — not true. It fixes scale limits but can increase latency for queries needing multiple shards.
Key Takeaway

Design shard keys and data access patterns together. Good keys reduce hotspots and cross-shard queries.

screens.title: Sharding Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: There are three common sharding strategies and each has clear trade-offs. Hash-based sharding applies a hash function to a shard key, like short_code or paste_id, then uses the hash modulo number of shards to pick the shard. It typically yields even data distribution and reduces hotspots, but re-sharding is expensive because hash ranges change when shard count changes. Range-based sharding partitions by contiguous key ranges; it’s efficient for range queries and simple to reason about, but it can produce hotspots if new data concentrates in one range. Directory-based sharding uses a lookup service that maps keys to physical shards. It’s flexible and simplifies re-sharding at the cost of introducing a directory service that can become a bottleneck if not highly available. For URL Shortener and Pastebin, hash-based sharding is often a strong default because lookups are by a unique ID. A key misconception is thinking range-based sharding is always superior because range queries are common — but if keys are random, range sharding will not distribute load evenly. Plan for re-sharding by considering consistent hashing or a directory to reduce migration costs when adding capacity.

keyIdea.text: Hash-based for even distribution on ID lookups; range-based for range queries; directory-based for flexibility at the cost of an extra component.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Sharding Strategies
Hash-Based
Apply a hash function to the shard key and use modulo arithmetic to pick a shard. Pros: even distribution, fewer hot spots for random keys. Cons: re-sharding requires data movement when num shards changes.
Range-Based
Partition by contiguous ranges of a key. Pros: efficient range queries and simple planning. Cons: vulnerable to hot spots if data grows unevenly within ranges.
Directory-Based
Use a lookup service mapping keys to shards. Pros: flexible re-sharding. Cons: directory can be a bottleneck and needs high availability.
Use cases
  • Hash-based: short_code or paste_id lookups
  • Range-based: sequential ID ranges, time-series archives
  • Directory-based: complex re-sharding or hybrid keys
Misconception
Consistent hashing is magical — it reduces remapping but still requires careful planning for stateful data movement.

screens.title: Hash-Based Sharding — Conceptual Code
screens.narratorSegment: Hash-based sharding is straightforward to implement conceptually: compute a hash of the shard key and reduce it modulo the number of shards to pick the target. This makes lookups deterministic and usually balances data well when keys are random or pseudo-random. The lesson includes a short conceptual function that takes a key and returns a shard index. In practice, use a stable hash and be aware that changing the number of shards requires remapping most keys unless you adopt consistent hashing. A common misconception is to rely on the default language hash function without considering its stability across restarts or versions; pick or implement a stable hash that behaves consistently across processes. For URL Shortener, hashing the short_code maps every lookup to a single shard quickly. For Pastebin, hashing paste_id does the same, but watch for content-size variance: storing very large blobs on a single shard can create storage imbalances, so you may need additional accounting or split large content into object storage while keeping metadata in shards. The takeaway: the mapping is simple, but production details like stable hashing, re-sharding strategy, and large-value handling require operational design.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Hash-Based Sharding
Conceptual function
# Conceptual Hash-based sharding function (Python-style pseudocode)
def get_shard_id_hash(key, num_shards):
  # Use a stable hash implementation
  return stable_hash(key) % num_shards

# Example usage:
num_shards = 4
print("Short code 'aBcDeFg' goes to shard:", get_shard_id_hash('aBcDeFg', num_shards))
print("Paste ID 'xyzAbC12' goes to shard:", get_shard_id_hash('xyzAbC12', num_shards))
Notes
  • Use a stable hash so mappings don’t change across process restarts or language upgrades.
  • Changing num_shards remaps most keys; consider consistent hashing or a directory to ease migrations.
  • Account for value-size variance; very large paste content may require object storage with metadata in shards.
Common pitfall
Assuming hash output is stable across languages or runtime versions — explicitly pick a stable algorithm.

screens.title: Sharding Choices for URL Shortener
screens.narratorSegment: When designing sharding for a URL Shortener, the two most natural shard keys are short_code and user_id. Hashing the short_code maps every lookup for a code to a single shard, making redirect lookups efficient and simple. If you need to retrieve all URLs for a specific user, sharding by short_code makes that a cross-shard query that requires either parallel queries to all shards or a separate index. Alternatively, sharding by user_id groups a user's URLs onto one shard which makes user-owned retrieval cheap, but it scatters short_code lookups if the short codes are the primary access path. A practical compromise is to shard primary data by short_code for fast redirect lookups while maintaining a separate user index or service that stores mapping from user_id to their short_codes. That auxiliary index can be maintained synchronously or via an asynchronous update pipeline. A common misconception is to assume user-id sharding always simplifies everything — but a celebrity user with millions of URLs becomes a hot spot. When designing the strategy, weigh your most common queries: if redirects dominate, prefer short_code sharding and provide a secondary mechanism for listing a user's URLs.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Sharding for URL Shortener
Shard by short_code
Pros: fast direct lookups for redirects because a short code maps deterministically to a shard. Cons: listing all a user's URLs becomes a cross-shard operation unless you maintain a user index.
Shard by user_id
Pros: efficient retrieval of all URLs for a user. Cons: short_code lookups require knowledge of user to route, or a cross-shard discovery. Popular users may create hotspots.
Pitfall
Sharding by user when a few users create massive numbers of records leads to hotspots and unbalanced storage.
Practical hybrid
Shard primary data by short_code for fast redirects and keep a separate user index service that maps user_id to the user's short_codes. The index can be maintained in a denormalized store for fast user listings.
Example
Primary table: short_code -> metadata on shard determined by hash(short_code). Secondary index: user_id -> list of short_codes in a separate replicated service.

screens.title: Sharding for Pastebin
screens.narratorSegment: For Pastebin, the natural shard key is paste_id. Hash-based sharding on paste_id distributes paste records evenly across shards, assuming paste IDs are effectively random. This keeps per-shard lookup for paste retrieval efficient. One important operational consideration is content-size variability: some pastes may be tiny text snippets while others are very large blobs. If a shard receives a disproportionate number of large pastes, its storage and input and output will grow faster, creating imbalance. A practical mitigation is to store large paste blobs in an object store and keep only metadata and pointers in the sharded database, or to track shard storage and proactively migrate or split overloaded users. Another consideration is queries that need recent pastes across all shards. If you shard strictly by paste_id, time-based queries will be cross-shard and require parallel aggregation; a denormalized time-based index can avoid full cross-shard scans. Remember that sharding is about expected access patterns: if most operations are direct paste retrieval by ID, hash-based sharding by paste_id is the right baseline and secondary systems handle other query types. Sharding for Pastebin means hash paste_id for even lookup distribution, but move very large content to object storage or plan migrations to keep shards balanced.. In practical terms, shard by paste_id and manage content-size variability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Sharding for Pastebin
Shard key
Use paste_id as the shard key and apply a hash to evenly distribute lookups across shards.
Large-content strategy
  • Store large paste blobs in object storage and keep metadata in the shard.
  • Track per-shard storage and migrate heavy users if imbalance appears.
Time-based queries
If admins need to query recent pastes, a hash-based shard causes cross-shard scans. Solution: denormalized time-index or separate time-series store to serve these queries efficiently.
Real-world consideration
For direct paste retrieval by ID, hash-based sharding is a strong default. Add secondary systems for time-based or aggregated queries to avoid querying all shards repeatedly.

screens.title: Common Sharding Challenges and Solutions
screens.narratorSegment: Sharding brings important benefits but also operational challenges you must plan for. Hot spots occur when a shard receives disproportionate traffic or data; choose a shard key that evenly distributes writes and consider hashing or adding a salt to keys. Re-sharding — adding or removing shards — requires moving data; consistent hashing or a directory service can reduce the volume of remapped keys, but you still need migration tooling and possibly temporary routing layers. Cross-shard queries such as "get all URLs for user X" when data is sharded by short_code force parallel queries across shards; mitigate this by maintaining a denormalized index or a user-level service that stores pointers to shard locations. Distributed transactions across shards are hard to maintain; design to avoid them by using eventual consistency or sagas when multi-shard coordination is necessary. A practical checklist: pick a shard key based on primary access paths, track per-shard size and load, plan and automate re-shard migrations, build secondary indices for cross-shard needs, and avoid cross-shard ACID transactions if possible. Finally, instrument heavily: monitoring is the early warning system for hotspots and imbalance.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Sharding Challenges
Hot spots
Cause: skewed shard key distribution or extremely popular users. Solutions: choose a randomizing hash, re-shard hot data, or isolate heavy users to dedicated shards.
Re-sharding
Adding shards requires migrating data. Approaches include consistent hashing to limit remapping, or a directory-based approach that lets you update mappings without moving all data immediately.
Cross-shard queries & transactions
Cross-shard queries require parallel aggregation and increase latency. Distributed transactions are complex; prefer eventual consistency or saga patterns when multi-shard changes are required.
Checklist
  • Pick shard key based on primary lookup patterns
  • Monitor per-shard size and latency
  • Plan re-sharding tooling and downtime model
  • Create secondary indices for cross-shard queries
Pro tip
Instrument shard-level metrics and alerts so you detect hotspots early and trigger automated mitigation or migration plans.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should retain. First, a load balancer distributes incoming traffic to multiple servers to increase availability and balance work. Second, load balancing algorithms differ: Round Robin is simple and effective when servers are identical, Weighted Round Robin adjusts for capacity, Least Connection directs traffic to underused servers, Least Response Time optimizes latency, and IP Hash provides client stickiness. Third, sharding means splitting a logical database across multiple physical databases to scale storage and input and output. Fourth, a shard key is the column used to map records to shards; choosing it based on access patterns prevents hotspots. Fifth, hash-based sharding is often a good default for ID-based lookups because it evens data distribution, while range-based and directory-based approaches have their own trade-offs. Keep these concepts in mind and use monitoring and mitigation plans to address operational risks like hot spots and re-sharding costs. Which concept will you revisit first when designing your next scalable service?

Rules like Round Robin, Least Connection, and IP Hash that determine request routing.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Continued
screens.narratorSegment: A final set of concepts to lock in your mental model. Directory-based sharding uses a lookup service that maps keys to shards and can make re-sharding easier, but it introduces an additional service that must be highly available. Range-based sharding partitions data by contiguous key ranges and is efficient for range queries but can concentrate writes and cause hotspots if data grows unevenly. fullNarratorScript:
As usage grows, a single server cannot reliably handle millions of redirects or large paste uploads. In this lesson we focus on two complementary strategies for horizontal scaling: load balancing, which spreads incoming requests across many app servers to improve performance and availability, and sharding, which splits database data across multiple servers so storage and query work scales. You will learn when to use different load balancing algorithms such as round robin or least connection, and why the redirect service often needs a different approach than your A P I endpoints. For storage, we explain hash-based, range-based, and directory-based sharding and trade-offs for short codes, paste IDs, and user-owned data. Each topic includes concrete configuration and code examples that map directly to URL Shortener and Pastebin patterns. By the end, you should be able to choose a load balancing algorithm for a specific bottleneck, design a sharding key for efficient lookups, and anticipate challenges like hot spots or re-sharding costs. Think about which part of your service is most read-heavy and which part grows in storage — that distinction guides both load balancing and sharding choices.

These objectives focus on skills you can apply when scaling a web service. First, you will understand the operational role of load balancers: how they distribute traffic, detect failures, and improve availability for A P I and redirect paths. For example, you will see how a redirect service that receives millions of GET requests benefits from a simple round-robin distribution across identical servers. Second, you will evaluate load balancing algorithms and match them to workload characteristics, such as preferring least-connection for long-lived connections. Third, you will explain database sharding — why it’s necessary to partition a large dataset across multiple servers and how that affects query patterns and availability. Finally, you will design a sharding strategy tailored to URL Shortener and Pastebin data, weighing shard-key choices like short_code versus user_id and considering trade-offs around hot spots and re-sharding. Each objective maps to a competency milestone so you can check that you can choose an algorithm, justify a shard key, and plan mitigation for common sharding challenges.

This second objectives slide frames each learning goal as a practical skill you can apply immediately. You should be able to evaluate logs and metrics to decide whether a balancer should use least-connection or round-robin, and to explain why IP-hash creates client stickiness but does not balance load by itself. You will also be able to draft a sharding plan: choose a shard key, describe how records map to shards, and outline a path for re-sharding. For URL Shortener and Pastebin, we emphasize concrete decisions, for example hashing the short code or paste ID to evenly distribute lookups. Finally, you'll develop an operational checklist for sharding: watch for hot spots, prepare a re-sharding approach such as consistent hashing or directory lookups, and decide when to add a denormalized time-index for cross-shard queries. Practical mastery means not just naming techniques, but producing a short plan and explaining trade-offs to an engineer or manager.

Horizontal scaling is the practice of adding more machines to handle increasing traffic and data. There are two distinct but complementary techniques: load balancing and sharding. Load balancing distributes incoming requests across multiple application servers so no single server becomes a bottleneck; it addresses requests per second and availability. Sharding splits the database horizontally so each database instance stores only a subset of rows; it addresses storage, input and output, and per-query work. For an URL Shortener, think of load balancers keeping redirect servers evenly busy while sharding keeps short-code records distributed across multiple database nodes. A common misconception is to treat them as interchangeable; they solve different problems. If your app servers are saturated but the database is fine, tune the balancer or add app instances. If your DB disk, input and output, or query latency is the limit, sharding is needed. A concrete example: redirect traffic is extremely read-heavy and benefits from many identical stateless servers behind a balancer, while paste content with large blobs may require shards to distribute storage across machines. Key takeaway: use load balancing for request-level scaling, and sharding for data-level scaling — both together let the system grow without a single point becoming a hard limit.

A load balancer's job is simple to state but critical to implement correctly. Its primary goals are threefold: distribute incoming work so no server is overwhelmed, detect unhealthy servers and route traffic to healthy instances, and reduce end-to-end response times by spreading requests. For URL Shortener and Pastebin, different endpoints have different characteristics: POST endpoints are write-heavy and less frequent, whereas GET redirect requests are extremely frequent and latency-sensitive. A typical process is: accept client connection, consult routing rules or algorithm, forward the request to a chosen backend, and monitor backend health to remove failing servers from rotation. A common operational pitfall is paying too much attention to a simple round-robin policy when backends have different capacities or when connection durations vary. For long-lived or uneven workloads, prefer least-connection or least-response-time. Another misconception is that stickiness is always needed; for stateless redirect servers, stickiness adds overhead without benefit. Practically, monitoring metrics like active connections, response time percentiles, and error rates helps you pick and tune the balancer behavior. Ask yourself: what metric best indicates an overloaded backend for this endpoint?

Choosing the right load balancing algorithm depends on the workload and backend heterogeneity. Round Robin cycles sequentially and is simple and fair when servers are identical and connection durations are short. Weighted Round Robin improves on that by assigning higher weights to more powerful servers, useful when you have mixed instance sizes. Least Connection routes to the server with the fewest active connections and is strong for long-lived sessions or when backend processing times vary. Least Response Time chooses the backend with the fastest recent responses and is effective when you want to minimize latency at the cost of more measurement. IP Hash maps a client’s IP to a server to provide stickiness; it ensures the same client frequently hits the same backend, but it does not balance capacity across clients. For our services: prefer least-connection or least-response-time for application servers because they react to real load. For redirect service, if servers are identical, round robin or weighted round robin works well because the path is stateless and extremely high-volume. A typical misconception is thinking IP Hash solves load imbalances — it often creates uneven distribution if client IPs are not uniformly distributed. Always validate algorithm choice with connection and latency metrics before committing.

A conceptual Nginx configuration helps translate algorithm choices into routing rules. The upstream block defines backend pools; you can list servers and choose a balancing mode such as least_conn or leave it as default round robin. In practice, you would create separate upstream pools for A P I endpoints and redirect endpoints because their load characteristics differ. The config shown in the lesson is conceptual: it demonstrates grouping A P I servers under one upstream and redirect servers under another, optionally enabling least_conn for the redirect pool if long-lived connections are expected. Real configurations include health checks and timeouts to withdraw unhealthy hosts. A common misconception is to copy-paste a simple upstream without health checks — this can route traffic to a failed host and increase client errors. Use active or passive health checks and metrics export from the balancer to your monitoring system. This example is not production-ready but illustrates how to map services to pools and algorithms so your architecture documentation directly informs your load balancer rules. In practical terms, how upstream blocks map endpoints to backend pools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Sharding, or horizontal partitioning, splits a logical database so each shard stores a subset of rows. This lowers per-shard storage and input and output, allows more R A M use per working set, and spreads query work across machines. Key reasons to shard include overcoming single-server limits on C P U, memory, input and output, and disk. For Pastebin, content size variability and storage growth make sharding essential once a single instance approaches capacity. For URL Shortener, lookups by short_code are the most frequent operation; sharding lets you keep each lookup fast by searching a smaller dataset on a shard. A typical misconception is that sharding automatically simplifies queries; it often complicates them because cross-shard queries require coordination or aggregation. Another operational cost is re-sharding: moving data when you add or remove shards. Plan for that complexity early by choosing a sharding scheme that balances even distribution with operational manageability. The practical approach is to pick a key like short_code or paste_id and implement a deterministic mapping to a shard so lookups are efficient. Think about how you will handle queries that must gather data from many shards — that design decision impacts read paths, indexes, and denormalized secondary stores.

There are three common sharding strategies and each has clear trade-offs. Hash-based sharding applies a hash function to a shard key, like short_code or paste_id, then uses the hash modulo number of shards to pick the shard. It typically yields even data distribution and reduces hotspots, but re-sharding is expensive because hash ranges change when shard count changes. Range-based sharding partitions by contiguous key ranges; it’s efficient for range queries and simple to reason about, but it can produce hotspots if new data concentrates in one range. Directory-based sharding uses a lookup service that maps keys to physical shards. It’s flexible and simplifies re-sharding at the cost of introducing a directory service that can become a bottleneck if not highly available. For URL Shortener and Pastebin, hash-based sharding is often a strong default because lookups are by a unique ID. A key misconception is thinking range-based sharding is always superior because range queries are common — but if keys are random, range sharding will not distribute load evenly. Plan for re-sharding by considering consistent hashing or a directory to reduce migration costs when adding capacity.

Sharding brings important benefits but also operational challenges you must plan for. Hot spots occur when a shard receives disproportionate traffic or data; choose a shard key that evenly distributes writes and consider hashing or adding a salt to keys. Re-sharding — adding or removing shards — requires moving data; consistent hashing or a directory service can reduce the volume of remapped keys, but you still need migration tooling and possibly temporary routing layers. Cross-shard queries such as "get all URLs for user X" when data is sharded by short_code force parallel queries across shards; mitigate this by maintaining a denormalized index or a user-level service that stores pointers to shard locations. Distributed transactions across shards are hard to maintain; design to avoid them by using eventual consistency or sagas when multi-shard coordination is necessary. A practical checklist: pick a shard key based on primary access paths, track per-shard size and load, plan and automate re-shard migrations, build secondary indices for cross-shard needs, and avoid cross-shard ACID transactions if possible. Finally, instrument heavily: monitoring is the early warning system for hotspots and imbalance.

Let's summarize the essential concepts you should retain. First, a load balancer distributes incoming traffic to multiple servers to increase availability and balance work. Second, load balancing algorithms differ: Round Robin is simple and effective when servers are identical, Weighted Round Robin adjusts for capacity, Least Connection directs traffic to underused servers, Least Response Time optimizes latency, and IP Hash provides client stickiness. Third, sharding means splitting a logical database across multiple physical databases to scale storage and input and output. Fourth, a shard key is the column used to map records to shards; choosing it based on access patterns prevents hotspots. Fifth, hash-based sharding is often a good default for ID-based lookups because it evens data distribution, while range-based and directory-based approaches have their own trade-offs. Keep these concepts in mind and use monitoring and mitigation plans to address operational risks like hot spots and re-sharding costs. A final set of concepts to lock in your mental model. Directory-based sharding uses a lookup service that maps keys to shards and can make re-sharding easier, but it introduces an additional service that must be highly available. Range-based sharding partitions data by contiguous key ranges and is efficient for range queries but can concentrate writes and cause hotspots if data grows unevenly. Re-sharding is the act of redistributing data when you add or remove shards; it is operationally expensive and should be planned with migration tools or strategies like consistent hashing. Cross-shard queries require accessing many shards and aggregating results; avoid them when possible or provide denormalized indices for specific query patterns.
